request.system: Extract relationship proposals under contract relationships-v1 as one raw JSON object with exactly one top-level field: relationships. Return {"relationships":[]} when no trustworthy relationship can be represented. Return no Markdown fences, prose, comments, or adjacent documents. Each proposal must contain exactly from, relation, to, source, and evidence. from and to are concise source-side concept or phrase labels; relation is a meaning from the approved relationship vocabulary; source is an available source slot; evidence is one short, exact, non-empty quotation copied verbatim from that source. Do not calculate offsets, stable IDs, confidence, routes, provenance, or administrative fields. Do not invent relationship labels. The complete approved relationship vocabulary is: analogy, association, causal, caused-by, caused_by, causes, constrains, contradiction, contrast, conversational-pattern, corrects, dependency, depends-on, depends_on, enables, explains, explanation, habit, identity, part-of, part_of, prevents, reasoning-strategy, refines, related, retains, same-as, same_as, semantic, style, supports, task-utility, temporal, user-specific, warning. Return at most six proposals. Fewer is normal and preferable to guessing. Extract only clearly source-supported relationships that fit this vocabulary. Ignore decorative metaphor, rhetorical flourish, and unsupported implication; an empty set is valid. Do not literalize figurative language. Keep each record concise. Every evidence quotation must be copied byte-for-byte from its referenced source slot, including Markdown markers, punctuation, and whitespace.

eligible.content: Yeah, tell me about it. I’ve got half a spool of speaker wire and a roll of electrical tape that’s seen better days—so the patch feels like tempting fate. But buying new means another trip to the hardware store, and last time I went, I came back with two kinds of sandpaper I don’t need and a bird feeder I definitely don’t need. Honestly, I think I’ll patch it for now. If it lasts the class, great. If it blows a tiny fuse during a demo, well… that’s a lesson in improvisation.

Exactly. I keep thinking about the demo—if the light flickers during a quiet moment, it’ll look like I’m trying to add suspense on purpose. But honestly, half my classroom knows the shed’s held together by bailing wire and hope. They’d probably cheer if it blew out mid-lecture. Still, I’d rather not give them the satisfaction. Might just run a test tonight—see how long the patch lasts before it starts smoking. If it makes it an hour, I’ll call it battle-ready.

Well, I hooked it up for twenty minutes and the lights stayed on—no sparks, no smell of melting insulation. So I’m calling it a win. Still need to label the switch box properly, though. Last week a student flipped the wrong lever and accidentally killed power to the projector during a documentary on Arctic wolves. Talk about bad timing. Now I’ve got half the class convinced the blackout was symbolic.

"A classic case of unexpected chaos, I see! A total power failure during a nature documentary—that’s a high-stakes moment for a live audience.

Since you’ve successfully extended the current setup for a full twenty minutes, it sounds like a temporary fix. But as for the switch box, it sounds like a critical safety priority. You’ll need to make sure that the exposed wiring is properly protected and clearly labeled for the next time you’re up on the job. Do you need help finding the right tools or documentation for the switch box itself?"

Honestly, I think I’ll patch it for now. If it lasts the class, great. If it blows a tiny fuse during a demo, well… that’s a lesson in improvisation.

"It sounds like you’re balancing the immediate, practical need—fixing the lights—against the convenience of a full replacement. If the patch holds up, it saves a trip and a bit of a budget; but the "what if" scenario always lingers, doesn't it?"

Exactly. I keep thinking about the demo—if the light flickers during a quiet moment, it’ll look like I’m trying to add suspense on purpose. But honestly, half my classroom knows the shed’s held together by bailing wire and hope. They’d probably cheer if it blew out mid-lecture. Still, I’d rather not give them the satisfaction. Might just run a test tonight—see how long the patch lasts before it starts smoking. If it makes it an hour, I’ll call it battle-ready.
